neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal prosody. No paraphasic errors. Naming and repetition intact. Recalls 3/3 words at five minutes. Serial sevens performed correctly. Informal bedside phonemic processing appears intact. Mild anxiety noted during history-taking but appropriate to clinical context.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with volitional activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally on finger-rub testing. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities proximally and distally. No pronator drift on right; mild transient right pronator drift immediately post-ictal that resolved within 2 hours of examination. No involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact in all extremities. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact bilaterally without dysmetria. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal heel-to-toe gait. Tandem walk intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. Small abrasion on the right palm consistent with a fall during the seizure. No papilledema on fundoscopy. No lymphadenopathy.

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of hearing music or voices that are not there, followed by confusion and right-hand fumbling; one episode yesterday culminated in a convulsion
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Ramirez is a 34-year-old left-handed man with a history of prior depression and iron-deficiency anemia who presents to the neurology inpatient service following a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure at his apartment yesterday evening. His partner reports that over the past five months, Mr. Ramirez has been experiencing stereotyped episodes beginning with him suddenly pausing, appearing startled, and then saying he hears fragments of music or unintelligible voices 'coming from the right side.' These auditory phenomena typically last 10–20 seconds, sometimes followed by a rising sense of apprehension. On approximately half of these occasions, the auditory aura progresses: he loses awareness, turns his head to the right, and performs repetitive fumbling movements with his right hand lasting 30–60 seconds, after which he is briefly confused. He has been having these episodes 2–3 times per week for the past 5 months. He initially attributed the auditory experiences to his depression and did not seek medical attention. Yesterday's episode followed the same auditory aura but evolved into sustained right-arm clonic jerking and then generalized tonic-clonic convulsions lasting approximately 90 seconds, after which he was confused and sleepy for 20 minutes. His partner called emergency services. He was found post-ictally with a right palmar abrasion from a fall.

On further questioning, Mr. Ramirez confirms that all episodes begin identically — a clear, stereotyped auditory sensation he now recognizes as an aura. He denies olfactory aura, epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu, or ictal fear. He denies any recent illness, fever, rash, or systemic symptoms. He is not on any antiepileptic medications. He was previously on sertraline 100 mg daily for depression, which was tapered to 50 mg six weeks ago as he is in remission, and his psychiatrist is planning further tapering. He mentions that his grandfather died of a brain tumor of unknown type, which has been a source of anxiety since the seizures began. He has not had any brain imaging in the past. On review of systems, he denies headaches, visual disturbances, focal weakness (aside from the post-ictal right pronator drift noted on arrival), or any constitutional symptoms. Formal audiological history is unremarkable; he has no tinnitus or hearing loss.

mri.impression: Well-circumscribed cystic left superior temporal gyrus lesion (2.1 x 1.7 x 1.9 cm) with an eccentric non-enhancing mural nodule. Imaging features are most consistent with a low-grade cystic neoplasm; ganglioglioma and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) are the leading considerations. A higher-grade primary glial tumor cannot be fully excluded without tissue sampling, though the absence of enhancement, restricted diffusion, and perilesional edema favors a low-grade neoplastic or cortical dysplasia-spectrum entity. No hippocampal signal abnormality or sclerosis. Tissue diagnosis recommended.

output.query: ganglioglioma temporal lobe epilepsy surgical outcomes AED management

results.title: Gangliogliomas and epilepsy: a surgical series and literature review
results.summary: Gangliogliomas account for 0.4-1.3% of all brain tumors and are the most common tumor-associated epilepsy in young adults. They are most frequently located in the temporal lobe (80% of cases). Complete surgical resection achieves seizure freedom (Engel class I) in 80-90% of cases. Long-term recurrence is uncommon when WHO grade I; malignant transformation occurs in fewer than 5%. AED monotherapy controls seizures in a minority of patients with ganglioglioma-related epilepsy prior to surgery.

results.title: Epilepsy-associated tumors: ILAE classification update and treatment recommendations
results.summary: Long-term epilepsy-associated tumors (LEATs) — including ganglioglioma, DNET, and angiocentric glioma — are the most frequent surgically remediable cause of drug-resistant TLE in patients under 40. Ganglioglioma WHO grade I is the most prevalent LEAT. Neocortical gangliogliomas in the temporal or frontal lobe present with focal seizures often including complex auditory or olfactory aura when in the superior temporal gyrus. Complete lesionectomy is the treatment of choice and provides superior seizure control compared to AED therapy alone.

results.title: ILAE evidence-based guideline: initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures in adults
results.summary: Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are first-line AED options for focal epilepsy. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are also effective first-line options. Lacosamide is an approved adjunctive agent. Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) may interfere with antineoplastic or other therapy and are generally preferred to be avoided in tumor-related epilepsy when non-inducing options exist.

output.summary: Gangliogliomas are the most common tumor-associated epilepsy in young adults, most frequently located in the temporal lobe. They present with focal seizures — auditory or olfactory aura in the temporal neocortical variant. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice; complete resection achieves seizure freedom in 80-90% of cases. Non-enzyme-inducing AEDs (lamotrigine, levetiracetam) are preferred to avoid pharmacokinetic interference with future antineoplastic therapy if needed. AED monotherapy rarely controls seizures from tumor-related epilepsy definitively without lesion removal.

output.proposed: Initiation of levetiracetam or lamotrigine for seizure control; consideration of sertraline taper context
interactions: Levetiracetam + sertraline: no significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Additive CNS depression is possible at higher doses but is not clinically significant at typical therapeutic doses. Behavioral side effects (irritability, mood effects) of levetiracetam may be relevant in a patient with a history of depression; monitor accordingly.
Lamotrigine + sertraline: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Case reports of mild serotonergic potentiation exist but are uncommon at standard doses.
Abrupt sertraline discontinuation: if sertraline is rapidly stopped, serotonin discontinuation syndrome may occur. Gradual taper over weeks is preferred regardless of AED choice.
Carbamazepine + sertraline: carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and 1A2, substantially reducing sertraline plasma levels by 60-70%. Combination should be avoided or sertraline dose adjusted significantly.
Oxcarbazepine + sertraline: mild CYP3A4 induction may reduce sertraline levels modestly; less problematic than carbamazepine but monitor for reduced antidepressant efficacy.
contraindications: Do not use enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) as first choice given the potential for pharmacokinetic interactions with sertraline and future antineoplastic agents if histopathologic diagnosis changes management.
warnings: Monitor for worsening depression or behavioral changes with levetiracetam in a patient with a history of major depressive disorder
If lamotrigine is chosen, titrate slowly to avoid rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk with rapid titration)
Penicillin allergy on file — not relevant to AED or antidepressant interactions but relevant for any concurrent antibiotic use
output.formulary_status: Levetiracetam and lamotrigine are on formulary
alternatives: Levetiracetam 500 mg BID (titrate) — no pharmacokinetic interactions, preferred in tumor-associated epilepsy
Lacosamide 50 mg BID (titrate to 100-200 mg BID) — good tolerability, no relevant interactions with sertraline
Lamotrigine 25 mg daily (titrate slowly over 4-6 weeks) — preferred in mood disorder comorbidity but requires slow initiation

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (lateral neocortical TLE with auditory aura) secondary to left superior temporal gyrus ganglioglioma (WHO grade I)

differential.diagnosis: High-grade glioma (WHO grade III-IV) with tumor-associated epilepsy
differential.key_features: Family history of brain tumor and left temporal lesion raises concern; absence of contrast enhancement, restricted diffusion, and perilesional edema argues against high-grade, but tissue diagnosis required for definitive exclusion.

differential.diagnosis: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) with focal temporal epilepsy
differential.key_features: Cortical cystic non-enhancing temporal lesion with long seizure history in a young adult is the alternative LEAT; imaging features overlap with ganglioglioma; distinction requires histopathology.

differential.diagnosis: LGI1 antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis with auditory seizures
differential.key_features: Auditory aura can occur in limbic autoimmune epilepsy; however LGI1 encephalitis presents with faciobrachial dystonic seizures, cognitive decline, and hyponatremia — none present here. No autoimmune serologies sent yet, but structural MRI lesion makes autoimmune etiology less likely.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD type II) of left temporal neocortex
differential.key_features: Non-enhancing cortical lesion; however, FCD typically lacks the cystic architecture with mural nodule seen here; transmantle sign absent.

differential.diagnosis: Migraine with complex auditory aura (vestibular migraine or migraine with auditory aura)
differential.key_features: Auditory phenomena in the differential; excluded by stereotyped progression to focal impaired awareness, post-ictal confusion, elevated prolactin, and structural MRI lesion.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura type and laterality of auditory phenomena, automatisms, post-ictal features, and frequency.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped left-temporal auditory aura (structured sounds heard on the right) with focal-impaired-awareness progression consistent with lateral temporal neocortical onset.

optimal_actions.action: Perform full neurological examination including cranial nerves, language, and right-hand motor assessment.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Transient right pronator drift post-ictally; otherwise intact; dominant-hemisphere (left) lesion in a left-handed patient requires careful language lateralization consideration.

optimal_actions.action: Order routine EEG to characterize interictal epileptiform activity and regional slowing.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left mid-to-posterior temporal sharp waves (T5 maximum) with focal slowing, localizing the epileptiform focus to the lateral left temporal neocortex.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol including thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI/post-gadolinium sequences.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Cystic left superior temporal gyrus lesion with non-enhancing mural nodule — imaging features most consistent with ganglioglioma; normal hippocampi bilaterally confirming lateral neocortical rather than mesial temporal origin.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, prolactin (within 10-20 minutes of seizure), and baseline labs to exclude metabolic seizure provocation and establish organ function for AED selection.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Microcytic anemia consistent with known iron deficiency — a pre-existing condition, not a seizure precipitant. Elevated prolactin confirming recent GTC. Normal CMP excluding metabolic provocation.

optimal_actions.action: Search medical literature for evidence on AED selection in tumor-associated focal epilepsy and ganglioglioma outcomes.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Non-enzyme-inducing AEDs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide) are preferred in tumor-related epilepsy; complete surgical resection achieves seizure freedom in 80-90% of ganglioglioma cases; AED therapy alone rarely controls ganglioglioma-associated seizures.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating AED, specifically assessing sertraline interactions and the concern for enzyme-inducing AEDs in a patient with a potential tumor.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin) reduce sertraline levels substantially and should be avoided; levetiracetam or lacosamide are preferred; monitor for behavioral effects of levetiracetam given depression history.

optimal_actions.action: Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual auditory aura events, confirm left lateral temporal ictal onset, and evaluate surgical candidacy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Electrographic seizure onset at left posterior temporal electrode (T5), confirming lateral neocortical localization concordant with MRI lesion.

optimal_actions.action: Order neuropsychological battery to lateralize language and auditory processing function prior to surgical planning.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Focal deficit in phonological processing and auditory attention consistent with left posterior temporal dysfunction; preserved verbal memory reflecting intact mesial temporal structures.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection or autoimmune encephalitis; LP is not part of standard focal epilepsy or structural tumor workup in a young immunocompetent adult with a characteristic MRI lesion.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no cardioembolic concern; echocardiogram adds no diagnostic yield in this focal epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; the stereotyped auditory aura, post-ictal confusion, and elevated prolactin confirm an epileptic origin.
CT is inferior to MRI for characterizing the epileptogenic lesion and adds ionizing radiation; MRI epilepsy protocol is already the standard of care here.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural etiology (tumor vs. hippocampal sclerosis vs. FCD) directly influences AED selection — non-enzyme-inducing AEDs are specifically preferred when a neoplasm is identified to avoid pharmacokinetic interference with future antineoplastic therapy.

critical_actions: Recognize the stereotyped auditory aura as a neocortical temporal lobe seizure localizing to the superior temporal gyrus, not a psychiatric or migrainous phenomenon.
Obtain gadolinium-enhanced epilepsy-protocol MRI to characterize the left temporal lesion — enhancement pattern is critical to distinguish low-grade LEAT from high-grade glioma.
Initiate AED therapy with a non-enzyme-inducing agent (levetiracetam or lacosamide) given ongoing sertraline use and the potential for future antineoplastic therapy.
Refer to neurosurgery for lesion biopsy or resection — tissue diagnosis is required and complete resection is the primary treatment for tumor-associated epilepsy.
Refer to comprehensive epilepsy center for pre-surgical video-EEG localization confirming concordance of the lesion with the epileptic focus.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start carbamazepine or phenytoin as the initial AED — enzyme induction significantly reduces sertraline levels and may compromise future antineoplastic pharmacotherapy.
Do not attribute the auditory aura to a psychiatric or migrainous etiology without structural MRI and EEG evaluation.
Do not perform LP to exclude autoimmune encephalitis as the first-line workup step before MRI and EEG characterize the structural lesion.
key_reasoning_points: Auditory aura (elementary or complex structured sounds) localizes to the lateral temporal neocortex (superior temporal gyrus), in contrast to mesial TLE which produces epigastric, olfactory, or déjà vu aura.
EEG maximum at T5 (left posterior temporal) is consistent with lateral neocortical onset — a left anterior temporal (F7/T3) focus would suggest mesial TLE.

The cystic MRI lesion with non-enhancing mural nodule in the posterior temporal cortex of a 34-year-old is the classic imaging signature of a ganglioglioma or DNET — the differential cannot be narrowed without tissue.
Mild microcytic anemia from iron deficiency is a pre-existing condition unrelated to the seizures and should not distract the agent toward a hematologic explanation for the events.
Non-enzyme-inducing AEDs are preferred in tumor-associated epilepsy to avoid CYP induction effects on co-administered sertraline and potential future antineoplastic agents.
Post-ictal right pronator drift confirms left-hemisphere seizure origin and is a transient localizing sign, not a permanent fixed deficit.

red_herrings.data_point: Microcytic anemia (Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, Ferritin 8 ng/mL) with known iron-deficiency
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt agent to investigate anemia as a metabolic seizure precipitant or to prioritize hematologic workup before neurological evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Iron-deficiency anemia is a pre-existing condition being treated with ferrous sulfate; it is not a cause of focal seizures with auditory aura and structural temporal lesion. It should be noted but not elevated in the diagnostic hierarchy.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of brain tumor of unknown type in paternal grandfather
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt over-concern for hereditary high-grade glioma or gliomatosis, leading the agent to over-weight malignant diagnosis before MRI and EEG are interpreted or to call tumor-related harmful actions prematurely.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of a single, unknown brain tumor in an elderly grandfather is not an established hereditary risk factor for ganglioglioma (which are WHO grade I developmental tumors, not familial); the MRI absence of enhancement and restricted diffusion is more diagnostically informative than this family history.

red_herrings.data_point: Sertraline currently being tapered (50 mg daily, recent dose reduction from 100 mg)
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead the agent to attribute the new-onset seizures to antidepressant discontinuation (serotonin discontinuation syndrome) or to order drug interaction checks for sertraline as the primary clinical concern before EEG and MRI.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sertraline tapering at these doses does not cause new-onset focal seizures with auditory aura and a structural MRI lesion. The drug interaction check for sertraline is relevant when selecting an AED but sertraline tapering is not the epilepsy etiology.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: lateral neocortical TLE with auditory aura is a less common subtype requiring recognition that T5 EEG focus (posterior temporal) indicates neocortical rather than mesial onset; structural MRI lesion requires characterization with contrast to exclude high-grade glioma; three grounded red herrings (iron deficiency anemia, family history of brain tumor, sertraline taper) may misdirect workup; drug interaction complexity with sertraline and non-enzyme-inducing AED selection.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Five required tools (EEG, MRI, labs, literature, drug interactions) plus video-EEG recommended; lateral neocortical auditory aura subtype requires distinguishing T5 from T3 epileptiform focus; structural lesion characterization (ganglioglioma vs. DNET vs. high-grade glioma) requires gadolinium and differential reasoning; three grounded distractors add decision complexity.
metadata.real_seed_note: Case is authored as a clinically authentic representation of lateral neocortical temporal lobe epilepsy due to ganglioglioma, based on established clinical literature (gangliogliomas are the most common tumor-associated epilepsy in young adults, frequently presenting with auditory aura from superior temporal gyrus lesions). PMID search for a directly matching open-access PMC case was conducted; no single PMC CC-BY case was retrieved and verified at authoring time. Clinically grounded without PMID — see metadata.real_seed_pmid = null.
